title: Flat extension identifies extended localization Čech complexes
statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a small site, $\varphi:\mathcal O\to\mathcal B$ a morphism of sheaves of commutative rings, and $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ global sections of $\mathcal O$, with $r\geq0$. Assume $\mathcal B$ is flat over $\mathcal O$ [def-pc-flat-sheaf-modules] and $\mathcal O/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\mathcal O\to\mathcal B/(\varphi(f_1),\ldots,\varphi(f_r))\mathcal B$ is an isomorphism of ring sheaves. $C(\mathcal O;f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ denotes the extended alternating localization complex: its degree zero is $\mathcal O$, its degree $q$ for $1\leq q\leq r$ is $\prod_{i_1<\cdots<i_q}\mathcal O[1/(f_{i_1}\cdots f_{i_q})]$, and all other terms are zero. The differential is the alternating sum of localization maps, and its augmentation to $\mathcal O[0]$ is the identity in degree zero and zero in other degrees. For $r=0$ it is $\mathcal O[0]$. Define $C(\mathcal B;\varphi(f_1),\ldots,\varphi(f_r))$ by the same formula. The map induced termwise by $\varphi$, $$C(\mathcal O;f_1,\ldots,f_r)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Res}_{\varphi}C(\mathcal B;\varphi(f_1),\ldots,\varphi(f_r)),$$ is a quasi-isomorphism in $D(\mathcal O)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category, def-pc-quasi-iso-modules]. Here module sheaves and restriction of scalars are [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category, def-pc-sheaf-restrict-scalars].

proof.text: For a product $g$ of the $f_j$, interpret $\mathcal O[1/g]$ as the sheaf associated to $U\mapsto\mathcal O(U)[1/g|_U]$. The maps $a/g^k\otimes b\mapsto\varphi(a)b/\varphi(g)^k$ and $b/\varphi(g)^k\mapsto (1/g^k)\otimes b$ give inverse scalar-extension maps after sheafification, by the tensor definition. Finite products here are finite direct sums, so tensoring the source complex with $\mathcal B$ gives the target; these formulas commute with every localization map and with the degree-zero identity augmentation.

proof.text: Use the following explicit cochain Koszul model, avoiding any implicit conversion from chain to cochain degrees. Put $K_n^q=\bigoplus_{|I|=q}\mathcal O e_I$ for subsets $I\subset\{1,\ldots,r\}$, $n\geq1$, and zero outside $0\leq q\leq r$. Set $a(j,I)=|\{i\in I:i<j\}|$ and $d_n(e_I)=\sum_{j\notin I}(-1)^{a(j,I)}f_j^n e_{I\cup\{j\}}$; the two orders of inserting distinct indices cancel, giving $d_n^2=0$. The transition $t_n(e_I)=(\prod_{i\in I}f_i)e_I$ is a chain map: the coefficient at $I\cup\{j\}$ in either composite is $(-1)^{a(j,I)}(\prod_{i\in I}f_i)f_j^{n+1}$. These sectionwise formulas commute with restriction and hence define complexes and maps of module sheaves.

source.place: Tag 0913 (more-algebra-lemma-extended-alternating-Cech-is-colimit-koszul), complementary-basis model in the proof

proof.text: For $g_I=\prod_{i\in I}f_i$ (empty product $1$), the map from the $I$ summand at stage $n$ to $\mathcal O[1/g_I]$ is $a e_I\mapsto a/g_I^n$. It is colimiting: every fraction has such a representative, and equality of two fractions means that multiplication by a sufficiently large power of $g_I$ identifies their representatives at a later stage. The colimit is computed by sheafifying sectionwise colimits; its differential coefficient is $f_j^n/g_{I\cup\{j\}}^n=1/g_I^n$, with sign $(-1)^{a(j,I)}$, exactly the alternating localization differential. Consequently $\operatorname{colim}_n K_n=C(\mathcal O;f_1,\ldots,f_r)$, and the identical formulas with $\varphi(f_j)$ give the target as $\operatorname{colim}_n(K_n\otimes_{\mathcal O}\mathcal B)$; the two identifications commute with the termwise comparison maps and augmentations.

Fix $j$. Define $h_j(e_I)=0$ when $j\notin I$, and $h_j(e_I)=(-1)^{a(j,I)}e_{I\setminus\{j\}}$ when $j\in I$. In $d_nh_j+h_jd_n$ every insertion of an index different from $j$ cancels with its removal in the opposite order; the remaining insertion/removal of $j$ has coefficient $f_j^n$, so $d_nh_j+h_jd_n=f_j^n\mathrm{id}$. This identity commutes with restrictions, and for a cycle $z$ gives $f_j^nz=d_nh_jz$, so $f_j^n$ annihilates every cohomology sheaf. For $r\geq1$, set $m=r(n-1)+1$: each degree-$m$ monomial in the $f_j$ contains some $f_j^n$, hence $\mathcal I^m\mathcal H^i(K_n)=0$ for $\mathcal I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\mathcal O$. For $r=0$, use $m=1$, since $\mathcal I=0$.

Here is the ideal-power torsion comparison needed in the preceding step, proved for sheaves rather than applied to section rings. If $\mathcal I\mathcal F=0$, the tensor universal property identifies $\mathcal F\otimes_{\mathcal O}\mathcal B$ with $\mathcal F\otimes_{\mathcal O/\mathcal I}(\mathcal B/\mathcal I\mathcal B)\cong\mathcal F$; the inverse is induced by the given quotient-ring isomorphism, and the identification carries $x\otimes1$ to $x$. Inductively, if $\mathcal I^{k+1}\mathcal F=0$, apply exact tensoring to $0\to\mathcal I^k\mathcal F\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal F/\mathcal I^k\mathcal F\to0$; the left term is killed by $\mathcal I$ and the right term by $\mathcal I^k$, so the outer canonical maps are isomorphisms, and a kernel/cokernel diagram chase makes the middle one an isomorphism. Thus $\mathcal F\to\mathcal F\otimes_{\mathcal O}\mathcal B$ is an isomorphism for every $\mathcal F$ killed by any positive power of $\mathcal I$.

proof.text: Flatness makes $F=(-)\otimes_{\mathcal O}\mathcal B$ an exact endofunctor of $\Mod(\mathcal O)$ after restriction of scalars. Apply the exact-functor cohomology isomorphism to $K_n$. Since it is induced on kernels and images, the map on cohomology of $K_n\to F(K_n)$ becomes the canonical $\mathcal H^i(K_n)\to F(\mathcal H^i(K_n))$; steps 4 and 5 show this is an isomorphism. Hence each $K_n\to K_n\otimes_{\mathcal O}\mathcal B$ is a quasi-isomorphism, naturally with respect to the transitions.

The exact and faithful forgetful functor to abelian sheaves preserves filtered colimits. The cited general-site abelian-sheaf theorem makes those colimits exact; exactness and faithfulness of forget therefore imply exactness of filtered colimits of module sheaves. Applying the exact-functor cohomology comparison to the colimit functor on the abelian category of diagrams (kernels and images componentwise) identifies $\mathcal H^i(\operatorname{colim}K_n)$ with $\operatorname{colim}\mathcal H^i(K_n)$, compatibly with maps. The colimit of the isomorphisms from step 6 is an isomorphism, so step 3 gives the required quasi-isomorphism, respecting the augmentations. If $r=0$, the quotient hypothesis is $\mathcal O\cong\mathcal B$ and the complexes are concentrated in degree zero, which also verifies this edge case directly.
